title: Investor Renovation Contractor in Charleston, SC | Genstone
metaDescription: Charleston, SC investor renovations: peninsula single houses, West Ashley ranches and North Charleston rentals scoped around flood zones and BAR review.
intro: Renovating in Charleston means planning around water, wood-eating insects and one of the oldest historic review boards in the country. Tidal flooding and heavy rain reach streets on the peninsula and in parts of West Ashley, Formosan and native termites thrive in the warm, wet climate, and exterior work on many older buildings needs approval from the Board of Architectural Review before a single board comes off. Those conditions make scope accuracy more important here than almost anywhere else in the Southeast. Genstone Construction renovates houses for investors, lenders and servicers across the Charleston area, from upper peninsula single houses to post-war ranches in West Ashley and rentals in North Charleston and Summerville. We're based in Romeoville, Illinois, and here we coordinate vetted, licensed South Carolina contractors managed by a designated field manager. Each project starts with a free Pre-Offer Rehab Review that weighs the repairs, flood zone and review requirements against the after-repair value. Then you receive a line-item scope with draws tied to finished work, no upfront payment and a one-year workmanship warranty once you approve the finished project.
housingStock:
Charleston's peninsula holds some of the oldest housing in the country, and its forms still shape renovation work. The Charleston single house, one room wide with its narrow end to the street and long side piazzas catching the breeze, appears across Harleston Village, Radcliffeborough and Cannonborough-Elliotborough. Freedman's cottages, smaller one-story houses with side porches, line streets on the Eastside, Westside and upper peninsula. Many of these buildings date from the nineteenth century, sit on brick piers or raised masonry foundations, and contain heart pine framing, lime mortar, plaster walls and wood windows that have been repaired many times. Iron earthquake bolts installed after the 1886 earthquake are still visible on some facades.

North of the Crosstown, Hampton Park Terrace and Wagener Terrace developed in the 1910s through the 1940s with bungalows, cottages and period revival houses, typically on raised crawlspaces. Across the Ashley River, West Ashley grew after World War II, with Avondale, Byrnes Downs, Moreland and Ashley Forest filling with brick and frame ranches, some on slabs in low-lying areas and some on crawlspaces. James Island's Riverland Terrace mixes older cottages with later ranches. North Charleston, built up around the former Navy Base and port, has blocks of 1940s and 1950s cottages and ranches, while Summerville, Goose Creek and Ladson added large subdivisions from the 1980s onward.

For investors, those types bring specific costs. Peninsula houses spend on structure, piazzas, windows, rot repair, plaster and review-compliant exterior work. Bungalows spend on piers, framing, termite damage and systems. West Ashley and North Charleston ranches spend on HVAC, electrical, plumbing, kitchens and baths, and, in low areas, flood damage and drainage. Across all of them, flood zone status and wind-resistant roofing affect both the scope and the cost of insurance after the work is done.

commonIssues.title: Flood exposure and prior flood damage
commonIssues.body: Large parts of Charleston sit in FEMA flood hazard areas, and the peninsula's low edges and West Ashley's Church Creek basin flood repeatedly from heavy rain and high tides. Houses with past flooding may have replaced lower drywall, damaged subfloors, mold in walls or crawlspaces and rusted mechanical equipment. Before buying, check the flood zone, the elevation certificate if one exists and the property's flood history, since they affect insurance, renovation rules and resale. We review those factors during the Pre-Offer Rehab Review.

commonIssues.title: Formosan and native termites
commonIssues.body: Charleston has both native subterranean termites and Formosan termites, which form larger colonies and can cause serious damage quickly. Older houses on piers, porches, piazzas and anywhere wood meets damp masonry are especially vulnerable. Damage is often hidden behind siding, under floors and in wall cavities. Buyers' lenders typically require a CL-100 wood infestation report, so treatment and framing repair belong in nearly every Charleston rehab budget. We price likely repairs after inspection and document treatment for the listing.

commonIssues.title: Wood rot on piazzas, porches and windows
commonIssues.body: Charleston's humidity, rain and salt air are hard on exterior wood. Piazza floors and columns, porch railings, window sills, trim, siding and roof edges rot where water sits or flashing fails. On historic houses, repairs often need to match original materials and profiles to satisfy Board of Architectural Review standards. Replacing rotted wood with proper flashing, ventilation and paint systems is a core part of most peninsula and older neighborhood renovations, and it frequently costs more than investors new to the market expect.

commonIssues.title: Salt air and corrosion
commonIssues.body: Salt-laden air reaches much of the Charleston area, especially near the harbor, rivers and marshes. It corrodes HVAC condenser coils, exterior fasteners, flashing, metal roofing accessories and electrical panels in exposed locations. Equipment and hardware that might last many years inland can fail much sooner here. Rehab scopes should specify coated or coastal-grade HVAC equipment where appropriate, stainless or properly coated fasteners and regular maintenance, which reduces premature failures and service calls.

commonIssues.title: Hurricane wind and roof attachment
commonIssues.body: Charleston's hurricane exposure means roofs, windows and their connections to the structure matter a great deal. Older houses often lack the roof-to-wall connections that current coastal codes require, and older roofs may be nearing the end of their life. When a roof is replaced, upgrading attachment, underlayment and edge details improves resistance to wind and can affect insurance. We scope roof replacements with those details in mind and include any required permits and inspections.

investorMarket:
Charleston's investor market varies sharply by location. The lower peninsula and the historic neighborhoods south of the Crosstown are among the most expensive in the Southeast, and renovation projects there are usually high-end, review-heavy and suited to experienced investors with deep budgets. The upper peninsula, including North Central, the Westside, the Eastside and Hampton Park Terrace, has seen significant reinvestment, and flips there sell to buyers who want character close to downtown, the Medical University of South Carolina and the College of Charleston.

West Ashley offers a wide range of post-war ranches that work as flips in neighborhoods like Byrnes Downs, Avondale and Moreland, and as rentals in other areas, though flood exposure varies street by street and must be checked carefully. North Charleston, around Park Circle and the neighborhoods near the former Navy Base, has become a popular area for both flips and rentals, supported by employers such as Boeing, Joint Base Charleston and the port. Summerville, Goose Creek and Ladson provide suburban rental stock with newer construction.

Small multifamily includes single houses divided into apartments on the peninsula, duplexes in North Charleston and West Ashley, and some fourplexes from the 1960s and 1970s. REO properties appear across the metro, often with storm, flood or termite damage. In every strategy, flood zone, insurance cost and wind requirements weigh heavily in the numbers.
permits:
The City of Charleston's permitting and building inspections staff issue building, electrical, plumbing and mechanical permits and perform inspections for properties inside the city, which includes the peninsula, West Ashley, James Island and parts of Johns Island. North Charleston, Mount Pleasant, Summerville and other municipalities run their own building departments, and Charleston County Building Inspection Services handles unincorporated areas. Permits are required for structural work, foundations, roofing replacement, window replacement in many cases, additions, new or relocated plumbing and electrical, HVAC replacements, water heaters and decks. South Carolina applies statewide building codes with coastal wind requirements, and residential contractors must be licensed or registered through the South Carolina Residential Builders Commission.

Charleston's Board of Architectural Review reviews exterior changes to buildings in the city's historic districts, including window and door replacement, porch and piazza work, siding, roofing materials, additions and demolition, and its staff can approve some minor work. Properties in FEMA flood hazard areas must meet floodplain rules, and substantial improvement or substantial damage determinations can require raising the house or bringing it into compliance. Genstone's field manager coordinates permit applications, BAR submissions, floodplain review, inspections and lien waivers from every trade.
climate: Charleston's climate is subtropical, with long, hot, humid summers and short, mild winters. Humidity drives mold growth, wood rot and termite activity, and it keeps crawlspaces damp much of the year. Hurricane season runs from June through November, bringing the risk of high winds, storm surge and heavy rain, and Hugo in 1989 remains the benchmark storm for the area. Tidal flooding during king tides and heavy summer downpours affects low streets on the peninsula and in parts of West Ashley. Freezes are rare but do occur, and vacant houses with exposed plumbing can be damaged. Exterior work such as roofing and painting is most productive in spring and fall, though hurricane season planning matters for any project with an open roof or walls between June and November.

faqs.q: Does Genstone have an office in Charleston?
faqs.a: No. Genstone Construction is headquartered in Romeoville, Illinois, and doesn't maintain a Charleston office. We coordinate a network of vetted, licensed and insured South Carolina contractors across the Charleston area, and each project has a designated field manager who handles scope, schedule, permits, BAR coordination and inspections. You receive photos and milestones as work progresses, which helps out-of-state investors and institutional clients manage Lowcountry projects remotely.

faqs.q: What does a Charleston Pre-Offer Rehab Review cover?
faqs.a: We look at the factors that drive Charleston budgets: flood zone and flood history, termite damage and the likely CL-100 outcome, wood rot on piazzas, porches and windows, roof condition and wind attachment, HVAC condition in a salt-air environment and whether the property falls under Board of Architectural Review jurisdiction. We estimate the repair cost, check the after-repair value against nearby sales and tell you whether the numbers support your offer.

faqs.q: Do you work in North Charleston, Summerville and Mount Pleasant?
faqs.a: Yes. Our Charleston-area work includes North Charleston, Mount Pleasant, Summerville, Goose Creek, Hanahan, Ladson and the islands. Each municipality has its own building department and rules, and we work with the correct office for every property. The process stays the same: free Pre-Offer Rehab Review, line-item estimate with a draw schedule, a designated field manager and payment tied to completed work.

faqs.q: How does flood zone status affect a Charleston renovation?
faqs.a: In a FEMA flood hazard area, the renovation must follow floodplain rules, and if improvements or damage repairs are considered substantial, the house may need to be raised or otherwise brought into compliance. Flood zone also affects insurance cost, which matters for resale and rental returns. We review the flood zone and any available elevation information during the Pre-Offer Rehab Review so you understand the implications before buying.

fix-flip.title: Fix and Flip Contractor in Charleston, SC | Genstone
fix-flip.metaDescription: Fix and flip renovations in Charleston, SC: upper peninsula houses, West Ashley ranches and North Charleston flips scoped for BAR, termites and flood zones.
fix-flip.h1: Fix and Flip Renovations in Charleston
fix-flip.intro: A Charleston flip has more ways to go wrong than most, and almost all of them can be priced in advance. Flood zone status changes what buyers can afford to insure, termite and rot damage hide under piazzas and siding, and the Board of Architectural Review controls exterior work on many older houses. Done right, though, a Charleston flip benefits from strong demand from buyers who want to live near downtown, the medical district and the water. Genstone Construction scopes Charleston flips with those factors on the table from the start. Our estimators price the work line by line against nearby renovated sales, often with more than one finish level, and a designated field manager runs the project with licensed South Carolina trades, coordinating permits, review and inspections along the way.

sections.h2: Upper peninsula flips and the Board of Architectural Review
sections.body:
Flips on the upper peninsula, in North Central, the Westside, the Eastside, Cannonborough-Elliotborough and Hampton Park Terrace, sell to buyers who value historic character and proximity to downtown, MUSC and the College of Charleston. Those buyers expect a careful renovation: repaired or matched wood windows, restored piazzas and porches, refinished heart pine floors and trim that suits the house, combined with modern kitchens, bathrooms and systems.

Many of these properties fall under the Board of Architectural Review. Window and door replacement, piazza reconstruction, siding changes, roofing materials, additions and some demolition require approval, and the board generally favors repairing original materials over replacing them. That affects both scope and schedule. We prepare BAR submissions early, design exterior repairs to match what is typically approved and build review time into the flip timeline. Interior renovation can usually begin while exterior approvals are pending, which helps keep carrying costs in check. We plan the sequence so the review never becomes the critical path.

sections.h2: West Ashley and North Charleston flips
sections.body:
West Ashley's post-war ranches in Byrnes Downs, Avondale, Moreland, Ashley Forest and nearby neighborhoods attract buyers who want a single-level house close to downtown at a lower price than the peninsula. North Charleston, especially around Park Circle, draws similar buyers along with employees from Boeing, Joint Base Charleston and the port. Flips in these areas need updated kitchens and baths, durable flooring, a functional layout and mechanical systems that are clearly new.

Flood exposure varies street by street in both areas. A ranch that sits on a slab in a low part of West Ashley may carry higher insurance costs and a history of water intrusion, which affects resale. We check the flood zone and evidence of past flooding during the Pre-Offer Rehab Review and adjust the scope accordingly, such as removing and replacing damaged materials, improving drainage and choosing water-resistant finishes at lower levels. Termite and rot repairs, HVAC with coastal-grade components and a roof built to current wind requirements round out a scope that holds up under a buyer's inspection.

sections.h2: Flood insurance, CL-100s and the closing
sections.body:
Charleston buyers look closely at flood insurance cost, the CL-100 termite report and the home inspection before closing, and any one of them can derail a sale. A buyer who learns late that a house sits in a high-risk flood zone may walk away or demand a lower price. An active termite infestation or untreated damage on the CL-100 can stall the lender. An inspection that finds rot under the piazza or an old roof without proper attachment invites repair demands.

We address those items before they become problems. Termite treatment and framing repairs are documented. Rot repairs are completed with proper flashing and paint. Roofs are replaced with current attachment details when needed. When a house has an elevation certificate or flood mitigation features, we include that documentation in the package your listing agent shares. Money is released only for finished stages, and you see the photos and inspection results as they come in. Genstone Financial offers fix-and-flip loans and credit lines if you want the money and the construction under one roof, but your own lender is welcome.

faqs.q: How long does Board of Architectural Review approval take?
faqs.a: It depends on the scope and whether staff can approve the work or it needs to go before the board. Minor repairs that match existing materials are often handled by staff, while window replacement, additions and significant changes go through the full board process. We prepare submissions early and build the review period into the schedule, and interior work can usually proceed while exterior approvals are pending.

faqs.q: Should I avoid flood zone properties for a Charleston flip?
faqs.a: Not necessarily, but you should understand the implications. Flood zone status affects buyer insurance costs and can limit the buyer pool, and substantial renovations may trigger floodplain compliance requirements. Some flood zone properties still sell well, especially in desirable neighborhoods. We review the flood zone and any history during the Pre-Offer Rehab Review so you can factor those costs into your offer.

faqs.q: Do you handle flips in Summerville and Goose Creek?
faqs.a: Yes. We work across the Charleston metro, including Summerville, Goose Creek, Ladson, Hanahan and Mount Pleasant. Each municipality has its own permitting office, and we handle permits through the correct jurisdiction. Flips in those suburbs typically involve newer construction with fewer historic or structural issues, so the focus shifts to roofs, HVAC, kitchens, baths and flooring. Summerville's older downtown streets are the exception, where cottages and bungalows bring back some of the termite and rot work typical of the city.

brrrr.title: BRRRR Rehab Contractor in Charleston, SC | Genstone
brrrr.metaDescription: BRRRR renovations in Charleston, SC: North Charleston and West Ashley houses rehabbed to appraise, with flood, termite and salt-air risks priced up front.
brrrr.intro: Charleston's rental demand is deep, driven by MUSC, the College of Charleston, Joint Base Charleston, Boeing, the port and a steady stream of new residents. The challenge for BRRRR investors is cost: purchase prices are high in much of the metro, and insurance can weigh heavily on DSCR calculations, especially in flood zones. The deals that work tend to be in North Charleston, parts of West Ashley and the suburbs, where purchase prices leave room for renovation and renovated comps support the refinance. Genstone Construction renovates BRRRR properties across the Charleston area to reach the appraisal and hold up to tenants in a coastal climate. A designated field manager runs each project with licensed South Carolina trades, and every repair is documented for your refinance lender.

sections.h2: Where BRRRR still works around Charleston
sections.body:
BRRRR deals around Charleston usually come from areas with moderate purchase prices and solid rental demand. North Charleston neighborhoods near Park Circle, Chicora-Cherokee and the corridors serving Boeing and Joint Base Charleston are common choices, along with parts of West Ashley, Hanahan, Goose Creek, Ladson and Summerville. The peninsula and the most desirable West Ashley neighborhoods usually trade at prices better suited to flips or long-term appreciation strategies.

The Pre-Offer Rehab Review is especially important here because the risks are larger. We estimate the full renovation and compare the result with renovated sales nearby, but we also look at flood zone status, which affects insurance and DSCR calculations, and at termite damage, rot and roof condition, which can add significant cost. A house in a high-risk flood zone may still work, but only when the insurance cost is known before the purchase. We show you the numbers so you can judge whether the refinance is likely to return your capital.

sections.h2: Renovating for the Charleston refinance appraisal
sections.body:
Appraisers in the Charleston area compare your rental against renovated sales and rate its condition and quality. A house with a renovated kitchen and baths, new flooring, a new or recent roof, updated HVAC and electrical, and no visible rot or termite damage earns a stronger rating than one with partial updates. Evidence of past flooding, rotted exterior wood or old mechanicals can pull the rating down.

Our Charleston scopes target those exact deductions. For North Charleston and West Ashley ranches, that typically includes HVAC with corrosion-resistant components, roof replacement built to current wind requirements, an electrical panel upgrade, PEX supply lines, termite treatment and repair, exterior rot repair, kitchen and bath renovation and durable flooring. We provide an appraisal package with permit records, final inspections, the CL-100, an improvement list, before-and-after photos and any elevation certificate, giving the appraiser documented evidence of the work and the property's flood characteristics. A recent wind-rated roof is also worth noting for the appraiser and the insurer.

sections.h2: Coastal materials that last in a Charleston rental
sections.body:
A Charleston rental faces humidity, salt air, heavy rain, termites and hurricane season, and material choices should reflect all of that. Inside, luxury vinyl plank handles humidity and pets, and in flood-prone houses it can be paired with water-resistant materials at lower levels. In the bathroom, an exhaust fan ducted outside and a tub surround with no weak grout lines are the two items that keep Lowcountry humidity from turning into mold. Kitchens get durable counters and cabinets.

Outside and under the house, the choices matter even more. HVAC equipment with coated coils lasts longer in salt air. Stainless or properly coated fasteners prevent rust streaks and failures. Fiber cement or properly flashed and painted wood siding resists rot. Roofs built with current attachment and underlayment details hold up better in storms and may improve insurance terms. Termite treatment with a renewable bond protects framing, and gutters, grading and crawlspace vapor barriers reduce the moisture that draws termites and rots wood. These choices cost more at renovation and less over the life of the rental.

faqs.q: How does flood insurance affect a Charleston BRRRR?
faqs.a: Flood insurance can be a significant expense for properties in high-risk flood zones, and DSCR lenders include insurance in their calculations. A property that looks good on purchase price may fail the DSCR test once flood insurance is added. We review flood zone status during the Pre-Offer Rehab Review so you can get insurance quotes before committing. If the numbers only work without flood coverage, the deal usually doesn't work.

faqs.q: Are military and Boeing employees good tenants for Charleston rentals?
faqs.a: They make up a large part of the rental demand in North Charleston, Goose Creek, Hanahan and Summerville. Military tenants may move on orders, which can shorten tenancies, so durable materials and fast turns are valuable. We don't predict rents or occupancy, but well-renovated houses near major employers generally compete well. Many military and corporate transferees lease remotely before arriving, so clean photos and documented upgrades help a North Charleston or Goose Creek rental stand out.

faqs.q: Can Genstone coordinate the DSCR refinance?
faqs.a: Genstone Financial is the Genstone company that writes DSCR rental loans, fix-and-flip loans and lines of credit. Using them is optional. With any lender, we provide the itemized scope, permit records, inspection results, CL-100, photos and any elevation documentation needed for the refinance appraisal and underwriting. Having the CL-100 and roof documentation ready before the appraiser visits tends to prevent the most common follow-up questions on Charleston-area refinance files.

rental-renovation.title: Rental Property Renovation in Charleston, SC | Genstone
rental-renovation.metaDescription: Rental property renovation in Charleston, SC: rent-ready rehabs, turns and deferred maintenance for Lowcountry landlords and single-family portfolio owners.
rental-renovation.intro: Owning rentals in the Charleston area means managing a climate that attacks houses from every direction: humidity, salt air, termites, heavy rain and the occasional hurricane. A rental renovation that accounts for those forces lasts; one that doesn't generates constant work orders. Genstone Construction renovates single-family rentals across Charleston, North Charleston, West Ashley, Summerville, Goose Creek and the surrounding area for individual landlords, funds, REITs and other portfolio owners. Acquisition rehabs, between-tenant turns and catch-up maintenance are all built by vetted, licensed South Carolina trades under one Genstone field manager. Owners follow each job through photos and milestones, and every payment matches finished work. Our Lowcountry rental scopes are built around salt air, termites and storm exposure first, and finishes second.

sections.body:
A Charleston-area rental portfolio often includes very different properties: a 1950s ranch in North Charleston, an older cottage in West Ashley and a 2000s house in Summerville or Goose Creek. They rent to similar tenants but fail in different ways. The ranch needs HVAC, electrical and plumbing updates along with termite and rot repair. The cottage may need foundation and framing work. The newer house needs roof, HVAC and water heater replacements as original equipment ages, with salt air shortening the life of outdoor components.

We set portfolio specifications for visible and replaceable items, such as flooring, paint colors, fixtures, appliances and hardware, so maintenance teams stock fewer parts and tenants see consistent quality. Each house then gets a scope suited to its age, construction and flood exposure. After each project, we record system ages and equipment details in the property file, giving your property manager a basis for capital planning instead of guessing when the next condenser will fail.

Most Charleston rental calls trace back to a short list of causes: HVAC systems struggling with heat and humidity or corroded by salt air, moisture in bathrooms and crawlspaces, termites, rot and storm damage. Addressing those causes during renovation pays back through fewer calls.

We specify HVAC with corrosion-resistant coils where salt exposure is significant, size systems properly and seal ductwork. Bath fans are ducted outside and surrounds are chosen to stay watertight. Crawlspaces get vapor barriers and drainage corrections. Termite treatment with a renewable bond protects framing, and rot-prone exterior wood is replaced with properly flashed and painted material or more durable alternatives. Roofs are built with current attachment details. Inside, luxury vinyl plank, scrubbable paint and durable counters handle tenant turnover. Together, those choices reduce what the property costs to own year after year. On houses within sight of the marsh or the harbor, we also put outdoor equipment and exterior fasteners on a shorter inspection cycle, since salt exposure shortens their lives. Catching a corroded condenser coil or a rusted hurricane strap during a routine visit is far cheaper than replacing a failed system in August.

sections.h2: Turns, storms and make-ready in Charleston
sections.body:
Turn speed protects rental income, and Charleston's rental calendar includes busy periods around the academic year and military moves. Genstone Construction handles make-ready work across the metro, and our sister company Genstone Field Services supports portfolio owners with inspections, occupied maintenance, turns and code compliance. Turns here usually mean paint, floor repair or replacement, checking fixtures and appliances, cleaning and fixing tenant damage.

Day-one photos give your property manager support for any deposit deduction. When a turn reveals a larger issue, such as termite damage, rot under a window or signs of past water intrusion, we document it and price it separately. After storms, we can inspect and document damage across a portfolio so you can prioritize repairs and support insurance claims. Turn work is paid after it's done, and the one-year workmanship warranty applies to our repairs rather than tenant damage or normal wear. Portfolio owners can pre-approve standard turn pricing so routine make-ready starts as soon as keys come back.

faqs.q: Do you work with large rental portfolios in the Charleston area?
faqs.a: Yes. Genstone works with individual landlords and with investment funds, REITs, mortgage servicers and banks. For portfolio owners we standardize specifications, turn pricing and reporting across properties in Charleston, North Charleston, Summerville and nearby towns. Each house still has its own scope, budget and documentation. Owners with houses in Goose Creek, Hanahan or Ladson can use the same specification and reporting across those properties too, which makes comparing turn costs and system ages much simpler.

faqs.q: Can you help after a hurricane or tropical storm?
faqs.a: We can inspect and document damage across your Charleston-area rentals, prioritize urgent repairs such as roof tarping and water removal, and price permanent repairs. Thorough photo documentation supports insurance claims. Availability after major storms depends on conditions and demand, so planning ahead with a portfolio list helps. Giving us roof ages, access instructions and photos of each property before the season starts lets us triage faster when a storm does pass through the Charleston area.

faqs.q: What upgrades reduce costs in Charleston rentals?
faqs.a: The most effective are HVAC with corrosion-resistant components, sealed ducts, a renewable termite bond, crawlspace vapor barriers, exterior-vented bath fans, durable flooring and a roof with current wind attachment details. Those items reduce the most expensive and frequent work orders in the Lowcountry climate. Each item is priced separately, so you can phase them across a Charleston portfolio as houses turn rather than doing everything at once. We usually recommend starting with the roofs and HVAC systems closest to the end of their lives.

multifamily-renovation.title: Duplex and 2–4 Unit Renovation in Charleston, SC | Genstone
multifamily-renovation.metaDescription: Duplex and small multifamily renovation in Charleston, SC: divided single houses, North Charleston duplexes and West Ashley fourplexes, phased for tenants.
multifamily-renovation.h1: Duplex and Small Multifamily Renovation in Charleston
multifamily-renovation.intro: Charleston's small multifamily properties range from nineteenth-century single houses divided into apartments on the peninsula to mid-century duplexes in North Charleston and fourplexes in West Ashley. Each type carries its own challenges: historic review and old construction on the peninsula, flood exposure and aging systems in West Ashley and North Charleston, and termites and salt air everywhere. Genstone Construction renovates two- to four-unit properties across the Charleston area for investors who need shared systems upgraded, units modernized, tenants managed during construction and permits and approvals handled properly. A single Genstone field manager coordinates the licensed trades, and each payment follows completed work. Hurricane season and flood exposure are factored into the schedule and scope from the beginning.

sections.h2: Divided single houses on the peninsula
sections.body:
Many Charleston single houses and larger peninsula homes were divided into apartments decades ago, often with one unit per floor and access from the piazzas. These conversions frequently have shared or inadequate systems, limited fire separation, exterior stairs that have deteriorated and smoke alarm coverage that doesn't meet current requirements. Many sit under the Board of Architectural Review's jurisdiction, which affects exterior work like stairs, piazzas and windows.

Renovating these buildings starts with structure and life safety. Rotted piazza framing, failing stairs and damaged sills need repair. Fire separation between units, interconnected smoke and carbon monoxide alarms and code-compliant egress are essential. Separate HVAC systems and electrical panels for each unit improve tenant comfort and allow separate billing. Unit interiors follow, with materials suited to older buildings. Before purchase, confirm the legal unit count with the city, since some conversions were never approved. The Board of Architectural Review's approval is needed for most exterior changes on these buildings, so that review starts at the same time as permitting.

sections.h2: North Charleston duplexes and West Ashley fourplexes
sections.body:
The duplexes and fourplexes in North Charleston and West Ashley were mostly built as multifamily from the start, between the 1950s and 1980s. They tend to have simple, repeated floor plans, slab or crawlspace foundations, shared roofs and original systems that are failing together: HVAC units, water heaters, electrical panels, windows and plumbing. Termite damage and rot at doors, windows and trim are common. Some sit in flood-prone areas, particularly in parts of West Ashley.

Because the units mirror one another, the first scope becomes the template and materials can be bought for the whole building at once. We start with shared items such as roof, water service, sewer lines, drainage and exterior repairs, then renovate units together if the building is vacant or one at a time if tenants remain. In flood-prone buildings, we discuss water-resistant materials at lower levels and drainage improvements, and we review whether the scope might trigger floodplain requirements.

sections.h2: Phasing work with tenants and storms in mind
sections.body:
Many small multifamily properties in the Charleston area sell with tenants in place. We phase renovations so shared systems come first, with shutoffs scheduled through your property manager and completed quickly. Interiors follow as each apartment empties, with dust and noise contained for the neighbors and fire separation and alarms kept working.

Hurricane season adds another layer of planning. Projects with open roofs, removed windows or exposed walls between June and November need a plan for securing the building if a storm approaches. We schedule roofing and major exterior work outside peak storm season when possible, and we keep materials and equipment secured on site. Student buildings near the College of Charleston and MUSC often turn over together in late spring, creating a window for heavier interior work before the heart of hurricane season arrives. Payment tracks finished units, not calendar dates. If a storm forces a pause, the field manager documents site conditions before and after so the schedule and any damage are clear.

faqs.q: Do peninsula multifamily renovations need BAR approval?
faqs.a: Exterior changes to buildings under the Board of Architectural Review's jurisdiction need approval, including stairs, piazzas, windows, doors and additions. Interior unit renovations generally don't. We prepare submissions early and build review time into the schedule so interior work can progress while exterior approvals are pending. Where an exterior stair is unsafe, temporary measures can usually be put in place while the permanent design is reviewed, so tenants keep a safe way in and out.

faqs.q: Can you renovate a Charleston duplex with tenants in place?
faqs.a: Yes. We schedule shared work like roofing or water service replacement with advance notice and complete it quickly, then renovate units as they become vacant or on a schedule coordinated with tenants. Since a job around tenants runs longer, the plan and draws are set up that way from the outset. Your property manager receives the schedule and notice for each shutoff, and fire separation and alarms stay in service for occupied units throughout. We also plan around hurricane season for exterior work.

faqs.q: Can I use FHA 203(k) on a Charleston-area duplex?
faqs.a: Yes. A buyer who will occupy one of the units can use a 203(k) on a building with up to four. That can work for owner-occupant investors buying a duplex in North Charleston or West Ashley. Genstone is a certified 203(k) contractor and prepares the bid package and draw requests renovation lenders expect. Buyers should get flood insurance quotes early on any duplex in a flood zone, since FHA requires coverage there and the cost affects affordability. Your lender can confirm eligibility.

fha-203k.title: FHA 203(k) Contractor in Charleston, SC | Genstone
fha-203k.metaDescription: FHA 203(k) certified contractor in Charleston, SC: bids, consultant coordination and draws for Limited and Standard loans on Lowcountry houses.
fha-203k.intro: With purchase prices high across much of the Charleston area, the FHA 203(k) loan can help buyers afford a house that needs work by financing the renovation together with the purchase. It's especially useful for older houses in North Charleston, West Ashley and the upper peninsula that can't pass a standard FHA appraisal because of termite damage, rot, an old roof or failing systems. Genstone is certified as an FHA 203(k) contractor. We work with Charleston homebuyers, agents, renovation lenders and HUD consultants to prepare itemized bids and draw documentation, then complete the work with a designated field manager and licensed South Carolina trades. We also help buyers understand how flood zones and historic review affect a 203(k) project.

sections.h2: Limited or Standard 203(k) for a Charleston house
sections.body:
The Limited 203(k) finances up to $75,000 of non-structural work, and no HUD consultant is needed. For many West Ashley and North Charleston ranches, that covers a roof built to current wind requirements, HVAC replacement, an electrical panel upgrade, a PEX repipe, windows, kitchen and bath updates, flooring and lead-safe paint work. Minor termite and rot repairs may fit as well.

Structural or larger jobs go to the Standard 203(k), which carries a $5,000 minimum repair amount and brings in a HUD consultant to write the scope and inspect every draw. In Charleston, Standard loans are common on older houses with significant termite damage to framing, rotted sills or piers, structural piazza repairs and projects that reconfigure the floor plan. We assess the house during the free Pre-Offer Rehab Review and tell you which program it likely fits, so the loan is structured correctly. When a house sits under Board of Architectural Review jurisdiction, we also note which exterior items will need approval, since that can affect both the loan schedule and the scope.

sections.h2: Flood zones, historic review and the 203(k)
sections.body:
Two Charleston-specific factors can affect a 203(k) project. The first is flood zone status. Properties in FEMA flood hazard areas require flood insurance for FHA financing, and if the renovation is large relative to the structure's value, floodplain rules for substantial improvement may require raising the house or other compliance work. That can change the project's scope and cost considerably, so we review flood zone and any elevation information before the bid is finalized.

Charleston's Board of Architectural Review is the second factor. Houses under the Board of Architectural Review's jurisdiction need approval for exterior changes like window replacement, piazza repairs, siding and additions. The board often prefers repair over replacement, which affects both cost and schedule. We prepare BAR submissions early and build review time into the schedule the lender uses to set the completion period. Interior work can often start while exterior approvals are pending. Buyers should get a flood insurance quote early, since the premium affects whether the total monthly payment is affordable once the renovation is complete.

sections.h2: Working with Charleston lenders and inspectors
sections.body:
203(k) loans depend on clean paperwork. Lenders need an itemized bid from a licensed contractor, and on Standard loans the bid must match the consultant's work write-up. Our estimators itemize labor and materials, then work through any differences with the HUD consultant before the loan heads to underwriting.

As each stage wraps up we request the draw, and on Standard loans the consultant inspects before the lender pays. The City of Charleston or the appropriate municipality issues permits and performs code inspections, and the final inspection needs to be complete before the last draw. We manage permits, BAR approvals, inspections, the CL-100 and lien waivers from every trade. Buyers and agents see progress through photos and milestones, and final payment comes after the homeowner approves the finished work. Because hurricane season can interrupt exterior work, we sequence roofing and window replacement to close the house in quickly, and we keep the lender informed if a storm delays the schedule. Termite treatment and the CL-100 are coordinated early so the lender isn't waiting on that report at closeout.

faqs.q: Can a 203(k) cover termite damage in Charleston?
faqs.a: Yes. Treatment and the framing repairs that follow can both go into the loan. Minor damage may fit within the Limited 203(k), while extensive structural damage usually requires the Standard program and a HUD consultant. Formosan termites can cause significant hidden damage, so the contingency reserve is especially important on older Charleston houses. We document the damage with photos as it's uncovered and submit change orders through the lender, so the buyer approves any added cost before work continues.

faqs.q: Does a flood zone rule out a 203(k) in Charleston?
faqs.a: No, but it adds requirements. FHA requires flood insurance on properties in high-risk flood zones, and large renovations may trigger floodplain compliance. We review those factors during the Pre-Offer Rehab Review so the buyer and lender understand the full cost before committing. An elevation certificate, when one exists, helps estimate both insurance cost and whether floodplain rules are likely to apply. If the scope approaches the substantial improvement threshold, we discuss alternatives with the buyer before finalizing the bid.

faqs.q: Which Charleston houses fit the 203(k) program?
faqs.a: Look for a purchase price that leaves room for the repairs and a finished value high enough to carry the full loan. In the Charleston area, that often means ranches in North Charleston and West Ashley, older houses on the upper peninsula and some properties in Hanahan, Goose Creek and Summerville. Owner-occupied buildings of up to four units qualify as well.

reo-renovation.title: REO and Bank-Owned Renovation in Charleston, SC | Genstone
reo-renovation.metaDescription: REO and bank-owned renovation in Charleston, SC for servicers, banks, funds and GSEs: securing, repairing and documenting vacant Lowcountry properties.
reo-renovation.h1: REO and Bank-Owned Property Renovation in Charleston
reo-renovation.intro: A vacant house in the Lowcountry can deteriorate quickly: mold in a humid summer, termites in the framing, rot in exterior wood and storm damage that no one reports. Our clients here include mortgage servicers, banks, REITs, investment funds and other lenders, and Genstone is a preferred contractor for Government-Sponsored Enterprises. Across the Charleston metro, we coordinate vetted, licensed South Carolina contractors managed by a Genstone field manager who produces the documentation asset managers require: itemized bids, photo documentation, permit records, inspection results and lien waivers from every trade. Our executive team's REO experience shapes how we secure, scope and report on bank-owned properties in a coastal market. Flood zone status, historic review and hurricane season are part of every scope from the first visit.

sections.body:
Humidity is the biggest threat to a vacant house in the Charleston area. With power off or the HVAC disabled, mold spreads across drywall, cabinets and ceilings during the long summer. Roof leaks, clogged gutters and failed flashing add water damage, and termites continue working in framing. Exterior wood on porches, windows and trim rots faster without maintenance.

Storms add another layer. After a tropical system or heavy rain, a vacant house may have wind damage, flooding or roof leaks that go unreported until someone visits. Properties in flood-prone areas of West Ashley, the peninsula or North Charleston may carry water damage from past events. Theft and vandalism are also common, with HVAC condensers, copper and appliances as targets. A Charleston REO scope typically starts with securing the property, stopping water intrusion and treating termites, then moves to mold remediation, system replacement and repairs to make the house marketable or financeable.

sections.h2: Permits, flood rules and historic review on REO
sections.body:
Renovation work on Charleston-area REO goes through the City of Charleston, North Charleston, Mount Pleasant, Summerville, Charleston County or the relevant jurisdiction for permits and inspections. Properties in FEMA flood hazard areas face floodplain rules, and if damage or improvements are substantial relative to the structure's value, the house may need to be raised or otherwise brought into compliance. That determination can dramatically change the scope, so we review it with the asset manager early.

Bank-owned properties under the Board of Architectural Review need approval for exterior changes like windows, piazzas, siding and demolition. Code enforcement staff in each municipality handle overgrown lots, debris and unsafe structures, and we address cited violations quickly. For REO clients, we keep permit records, inspection results, BAR approvals, the CL-100 and lien waivers in the property file. Genstone Field Services can handle preservation, inspections and code compliance alongside renovation. That continuity matters when a buyer's lender asks about flood status or a past code case.

sections.h2: Choosing the right REO scope in Charleston
sections.body:
How much to invest in a Charleston-area REO depends on location, flood exposure and the buyer pool. On the upper peninsula and in sought-after West Ashley and North Charleston neighborhoods, buyers compare listings with renovated houses, so a fuller renovation can significantly improve recovery. In areas with more investor buyers or where flood exposure limits the owner-occupant pool, a repair-to-market scope may be the better choice.

A repair-to-market scope typically includes a sound roof, working HVAC, functional plumbing and electrical, termite treatment and repair with a clean CL-100, mold remediation, rot repair on exterior wood, safety items such as handrails and smoke alarms and lead-safe paint correction on pre-1978 houses. If the choice is close, we write up both a repair-to-market scope and a fuller renovation, itemized and photographed in the client's format, so the asset manager can weigh them. Flood zone status and any elevation information are noted on every bid, since they shape the likely buyer pool. Each bid reflects conditions documented at our walkthrough, including termite, rot and water damage that a drive-by valuation can't see.

faqs.q: Does Genstone handle GSE-owned properties in the Charleston area?
faqs.a: Yes. We're a preferred contractor for Government-Sponsored Enterprises and also handle Lowcountry properties for servicers, banks and other lenders. We follow their bid formats, coordinate licensed South Carolina trades and keep photos, permit records and lien waivers with each property file. A designated field manager is the single point of contact for each Charleston-area address, from the first securing visit through final listing photos. Flood zone and BAR status are noted in every file.

faqs.q: Can you assess REO properties after a storm?
faqs.a: Yes. After a storm, we can inspect bank-owned properties, document damage with photos, perform emergency measures like tarping and water removal and price permanent repairs. Availability after major storms depends on conditions, so a list of properties prepared in advance helps us respond efficiently. Detailed photo documentation also supports insurance claims and helps asset managers decide which properties to repair first. We note any new code, flood or structural concerns the storm created.

faqs.q: How do flood rules affect REO repairs in Charleston?
faqs.a: If a property is in a FEMA flood hazard area and the damage or planned improvements are substantial, floodplain rules may require raising the house or other compliance measures before it can be repaired. That can change the cost and the decision to renovate. We review flood status with the asset manager before finalizing the scope. We document the flood history thoroughly for buyers and lenders.
